title: Condensation, damp and mould in a closed-up winter room
summary: Breath, cooking, drying clothes and any unvented heater fill a closed-up winter room with water, which condenses on the coldest surfaces and grows mould within days. Keep humidity lower as it gets colder outside, air out briefly and often, and use a salvaged hygrometer or CO2 meter to check. Airing out never replaces a heater's fresh-air opening or a CO alarm.

steps.text: Find a hygrometer (weather station console, smart thermostat, dehumidifier or dial gauge) and check it with the salt test: stir about 125 ml (1/2 cup) of table salt into 50 ml (1/4 cup) of water in a cup, and seal the cup and the meter in a big clear bag for 8–12 hours, out of sun and draughts. It should read about 75%; write down the difference and correct every reading (CMHC humidity).
steps.warn: Keep the salty water off the meter; it damages it (CMHC humidity).

steps.text: Put the meter in the room where you spend most time or where the damp shows, away from any radiator, heater, register or chimney, and give it up to two hours to settle (CMHC humidity). Read it morning and evening.

Keep humidity lower as it gets colder outside: about 30% once it's below −10 °C outside (CMHC humidity), and never over 45% all heating season (CMHC moisture). Water or frost on the glass means it's too high for that window.

Air out briefly and often: open windows wide for about 5 minutes, 2–3 times a day, more during and after cooking, washing or drying clothes, and 5–10 minutes in the bedroom after getting up (UBA airing). Opening windows on opposite sides at once clears the air fastest.
steps.warn: Airing doesn't replace a fuel heater's own fresh-air opening or a working CO alarm. Never seal a room tighter to cut damp or save heat while a fuel heater burns in it.

steps.text: Cut the water at its source: lids on pots, firewood kept outside, laundry dried in one place you air hard, and no more unvented burning than you need (CMHC moisture).

Let the room's warm air reach the cold surfaces: beds and furniture 15 cm (6 in) off outside walls, closets on outside walls not packed to the ceiling and their doors open, curtains open by day (CMHC moisture). Where you can, get mattresses off the floor.
Every morning wipe water off glass and frames. Once a week check window sills, wall-to-ceiling corners, closets, behind furniture and pictures, and under mattresses.

Clean small mould patches (1 m² or less in all) with unscented soap and water and dry them fast, wearing an N95 mask, goggles and gloves. No bleach. Throw out mouldy mattresses and soft furnishings (Health Canada mould).
steps.warn: Keep infants, older people and anyone with asthma or lung disease out of the room while you clean (Health Canada mould).

notes:
## Why it happens

Condensation needs three things at once: too much water in the air, too little swap with outside air, and a cold surface (CMHC moisture). A closed-up winter room has all three. Warm air holds far more water than cold air, so when room air touches glass or a wall colder than its dew point, the water comes out as droplets or frost (CBD 1).

Heating one room and leaving the rest cold makes it worse. Unheated rooms and big swings in temperature give the damp more cold surfaces (CMHC moisture). Keep doors shut between the warm room and the cold rooms, so moist air doesn't drift in and condense there (UBA airing). The one exception is a fuel heater: if one burns in the warm room and its label wants a door ajar or an opening to the next room, do that, because its air matters more than the damp (MSU kerosene says to keep the door ajar to an adjacent room; ProCom's manual describes openings to an adjoining space).

## Where it shows up

- **Windows first,** and the edge of the glass before the middle (CBD 231).
- **Closets and cupboards on outside walls,** which the room's heat doesn't reach (CBD 231, CMHC moisture).
- **Corners where outside walls meet the ceiling** (CBD 231).
- **Behind beds, furniture and pictures** against outside walls (CMHC moisture).
- **Inside walls and the attic,** out of sight, showing later as mould, rot or stains (CMHC moisture, CBD 1).
- **Under a mattress on the floor.** It can act like a packed closet: a cold surface the room's warm air barely reaches (CMHC warns against closet contents packed against cold outside walls). Put it on slats, a pallet or a frame, or stand it on edge to air each day, and look underneath. A mouldy mattress can't be cleaned (Health Canada mould).

## Where the water comes from

| Source | Water it adds |
|---|---|
| A whole household | 10–50 L a day (CMHC moisture) |
| Family of four | 7–12 L a day; over 23 L on wash days (CBD 231) |
| A family's washing dried indoors | about 12 L (CBD 231) |
| Cooking on gas, extra | about 1.2 L a day (CBD 231) |
| A cord of firewood stored indoors | over 270 L as it dries (CMHC moisture) |
| Kerosene (paraffin) heater | about 1.25 L per litre of kerosene burned (MAWWFRS heaters) |
| Unvented gas or propane heater | about 30 mL an hour for every 1,000 Btu/h of input (ProCom manual) |

So a 10,000 Btu/h (2.9 kW) propane heater on high adds about 0.3 L an hour, or 7 L in a day: about what a family of four's breathing, cooking and washing adds on an ordinary day (7–12 L, CBD 231). The same flame also releases carbon dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide into the room (Beacon unflued); the damp is the part you can see. A New Zealand housing research group puts unflued gas heaters at up to 1 L an hour (Beacon unflued). Only heaters connected to a chimney or flue send their combustion products outside (MSU kerosene); everything else burns its water into your room.

## How dry to keep it

Normally 30–50%; when it's below −10 °C outside, about 30% (CMHC humidity). In very cold weather 30% or lower may be needed, and never over 45% all heating season (CMHC moisture).

Single glass fogs much sooner than double. The highest humidity before a window fogs, with the room at 21 °C (70 °F) and wind outside (CBD 1):

| Outside | Single glass | Double glass |
|---|---|---|
| −7 °C (20 °F) | 24% | 53% |
| −18 °C (0 °F) | 12% | 41% |
| −29 °C (−20 °F) | 6% | 32% |
| −40 °C (−40 °F) | 2% | 23% |

Old single-glazed windows will fog in deep cold whatever you do. Wipe them every morning so the sills and frames don't rot.

- Very dry air brings dry eyes, nose and throat (CMHC moisture). In deep cold that's the price of a dry room.
- A humidifier adds water and can grow mould itself (CMHC humidity).
- Dehumidifiers lose effect below about 50% (CBD 231), so in winter airing out is the tool.

## Mould and health

Mould starts within 48 hours where things stay damp (Health Canada mould). It irritates eyes, nose and throat, and causes coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and worse asthma. Damp and mould may also help bring on asthma, bronchitis, chest infections and eczema. Infants, children, older people, pregnant people and anyone with asthma or lung disease are most at risk (Health Canada mould).

- Up to three patches adding to 1 m² or less: clean them yourself with unscented soap and water, then dry fast. No bleach. Wear an N95 mask, goggles and gloves (Health Canada mould).
- More than three patches, or 1–3 m² in all: Health Canada recommends an expert look but says a medium amount can usually still be cleaned the same way with the same protection. A single patch over 3 m² is large and isn't a wipe-down job (Health Canada mould): with no one to call, close that room off and sleep elsewhere.
- Painting over mould doesn't kill it. Mould under paint means the plasterboard has to go. If it comes back, the water source isn't fixed (Health Canada mould).
- Mouldy mattresses, upholstered furniture and most paper usually have to be thrown out (Health Canada mould). See [Mould and damp](#browse/hazards/mold).

## Fresh air: how much

- About 7.5–9 L/s of outside air per person keeps body odour at a level most people accept, and indoor CO2 about 700 ppm above outdoors matches roughly 8 L/s per person (NIST CO2). Outdoor air is now over 400 ppm (NIST CO2), so that's about 1,100 ppm indoors.
- Health Canada's long-term limit for homes is 1,000 ppm averaged over 24 hours. As CO2 climbs, tiredness, headache and poor concentration become more likely (Health Canada CO2).
- A closed-up winter room won't get that much air all the time, and a room where anything burns must not be left that way. Short, wide-open airings swap the air fast without chilling the walls and furniture. A window left tilted open for hours cools the wall beside it until it grows mould (UBA airing).
- A fuel heater's fresh-air opening is a separate thing: keep open whatever its label asks for the whole time it burns. The per-person figures above cover breath alone; a heater adds its own gases to them. Don't tape windows, stuff gaps or close the room's vents to cut damp or keep heat in while one burns. For a kerosene wick heater, MSU quotes a Consumer Product Safety Commission rule (1982) of 1 square inch (6.5 cm²) of open window per 1,000 Btu/h of rated output, and the maker's label comes first (MSU kerosene) ([Heater labels](#guides/reference_heater_labels), [Kerosene heater](#guides/skill_kerosene_heater)).
- CO2 is not CO. A CO2 meter shows how stale the air is, and CO2 says little about pollutants that don't come from people (NIST CO2). Keep a working CO alarm in the room: [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## Meters from salvage

- **Hygrometers:** weather station consoles and outdoor sensors ([Weather station teardown](#guides/teardown_weather_station)), many digital and smart thermostats ([Wall thermostat teardown](#guides/teardown_wall_thermostat)), the humidistat in a dehumidifier, and plain dial gauges. Salt-test every one (step 1) and again once a year (CMHC humidity). Keep it away from heaters, registers and the chimney, and give it up to two hours to settle in a new spot (CMHC humidity).
- **Real CO2 meters** use an NDIR (non-dispersive infrared) sensor. The Airthings Wave Plus, for example, reads 400–5,000 ppm to within about ±30 ppm ±3% at 15–35 °C once settled, runs on 2 AA cells, is rated for 4–40 °C, and takes about 7 days to settle (Airthings Wave Plus). Check the rated temperature on any meter you find; a room that drops near freezing at night is outside many of them.
- **"eCO2" or "CO2eq" is an estimate,** worked out from other gases, not a CO2 measurement: the SGP30 sensor board calculates it from hydrogen (Adafruit SGP30), and the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium shows estimated CO2 (ecobee 2022). Use them as a rough trend only.
